newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

text.p: Australian Meat and Livestock Corp's (AMLC) weekly export prices are as follows:

AMLC COMMENTARY: Australian beef shipments to Japan in February rose by 1,000 tonnes to 26,900 tonnes from a year earlier, representing about 45 percent of total shipments. This confirms the importance of the Japanese market to the Australian beef industry.

For the year so far, chilled exports are down by six percent while frozen exports are up by 20 percent. The decline in chilled shipments is almost totally attributable to the fall in chilled grainfed shipments, which are down by almost 19 percent.

Australian beef exports to all destinations in February were up by 1,500 tonnes compared with a year ago to just under 60,000 tonnes. Volumes increased to all major markets at the expense of shipments to other smaller destinations. Exports to the U.S. and Korea increased on February 1996 levels by 1,000 tonnes to 14,600 tonnes and to 4,500 tonnes respectively.

Export offer prices in Japan this week for Australian beef were firm to slightly higher across the broad range of product. Chilled grassfed fullsets were quoted at 124 US cents a lb but the appreciation of the Australian dollar meant that returns to Australian exporters were slightly lower.
The most positive news from Japan was confirmation that beef stocks were further reduced in January. At 95,000 tonnes, stocks are now at January 1996 levels, down from 140,000 tonnes in mid-1996.

Japanese beef consumption figures this week indicate the extent to which consumption was affected by the food safety problems of last year. After rising by seven percent a year in recent years, beef consumption in Japan fell by five percent in 1996 to just over one million tonnes. Total imports fell by 3.2 percent. Australia's share of the reduced market also fell by 3.2 percent to 45.4 percent.

In the absence of food safety scares, the Japanese beef market should resume growth again in 1997. This, coupled with an expected decline in domestic beef production, should help the imported beef market.

In the U.S., cow kills continue to be wound back as supplies drift lower. A strong rise in lean beef prices has been outstripped by increasing U.S. cow prices, slashing margins and forcing packers to reduce cow slaughter.

The largest price rises this week were for lean U.S. domestic product, which gained seven to 10 US cents a lb. Imported prices also continued to advance, by two to six cents a lb. A switch to fed cattle chuck and round cuts by U.S. grinders may temper further price rises for lean manufacturing beef.
Strength in the grinding beef market was not passed onto other sectors of the U.S. beef industry.

In Queensland, cattle prices more than regained last week's losses. The Queensland cattle market index now stands at 96.7 points, up from 91.1 last week, generally representing price rised of 8.0 to 9.0 cents a kg liveweight. In New South Wales

export cattle prices rose by about 6.0 cents a kg liveweight. In Victoria, cattle supplies remained heavy with yardings at more than 15,000 head. In 1996 yardings rose above 15,000 head only once. The availability of supplies subdued the Victoria market, with the state's bullock indicator increasing by about 1.9 cents a kg liveweight to 88.6 cents a kg liveweight.
Cow prices have improved in comparison in recent weeks but at 120 to 135 cents a kg dressed weight they are yet to fully reflect improvements in manufacturing beef prices in the U.S.
The last time time beef traded at these rates in the U.S., in March 1995, Australian cow prices ranged from 160 cents to 190 cents a kg dressed weight.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
